lead: A spar cap, a stringer or a fuselage frame is a beam, and the first questions are how much direct stress a bending moment causes and how much the beam curves. When the moment acts about a principal axis, one property, the second moment of area I, answers both: σ = M y/I and 1/R = M/(E I). The same bending also makes the cross-section curl the other way by the Poisson effect: anticlastic bending.
prereq: You need: the second moment of area and the parallel-axis theorem, and the bending moment diagram of a wing or fuselage (from the chapter on loads on an aircraft).

blocks.text: Bending is symmetrical when the moment acts about a principal axis of the section, usually an axis of symmetry. Simple bending theory rests on four assumptions:

items: Plane cross-sections stay plane and normal to the bent axis of the beam.
Deflections are small, so the curvature 1/R is close to d²v/dz².
The material is linear elastic, with the same E in tension and compression.
The moment acts about a principal axis, and no axial force acts.

blocks.text: The derivation follows from these in four steps:

items: A fibre at distance y from the neutral axis stretches by y/R per unit length, so the strain is ε = y/R.
Hooke's law gives σ = E ε = E y/R: stress grows linearly with y.
No axial force acts, so ∫σ dA = (E/R) ∫y dA = 0. The first moment ∫y dA is zero only about the centroid, so the neutral axis passes through the centroid.
The stresses must add up to the applied moment: M = ∫σ y dA = (E/R) ∫y² dA = E I/R, where I = ∫y² dA about the neutral axis. Put E/R = M/I into σ = E y/R.

blocks.text: σ/y = M/I = E/R,   σ<sub>max</sub> = M/Z,   Z = I/y<sub>max</sub>
blocks.where: σ is the direct stress (Pa) at distance y (m) from the neutral axis; M is the bending moment (N·m); I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis (m⁴); E is Young's modulus (Pa); R is the radius of curvature of the beam axis (m); Z is the elastic section modulus (m³) and y<sub>max</sub> the distance to the farthest fibre (m).

blocks.text: Doubling the depth of a rectangular section multiplies I by eight and y<sub>max</sub> by two, so the peak stress falls to a quarter. That is why spars are deep and skins thin.

sections.h3: Sign convention and sections that are not symmetric top to bottom

blocks.text: This unit uses one convention throughout: z along the beam, x horizontal and y upwards from the centroid, tension positive. Mx is positive when it puts the fibres at positive y in tension, and My when it puts positive x in tension. Then σ = Mx y/Ixx and the sign comes out of the formula. Upward lift compresses a wing's upper skin, so its root Mx is negative; so is the Mx of a beam sagging under a downward load.

A section not symmetric about its neutral axis, such as a T-section, has two section moduli, Z<sub>top</sub> = I/y<sub>top</sub> and Z<sub>bot</sub> = I/y<sub>bot</sub>. Yielding starts at the fibre farther from the neutral axis (the smaller Z), on whichever face it lies. The compression face matters separately, because thin compressed skin buckles before it yields (see the chapters on plate buckling and crippling).

A stretched fibre contracts sideways by ν ε, where ν is Poisson's ratio (about 0.33 for aluminium alloy, 0.3 for steel); a compressed fibre widens. In a bent beam the strain is y/R, so the sideways strain is −ν y/R: it changes sign across the depth. The tension side narrows and the compression side widens, and the cross-section curls in its own plane with the opposite sense to the bending.

blocks.where: R′ is the transverse (anticlastic) radius of curvature of the cross-section (m); R is the radius of the beam axis (m); ν is Poisson's ratio.

blocks.text: For aluminium R′ is about three times R: bend a rubber eraser and its end face stops being rectangular. The bar becomes a saddle.

The curl is free only on a narrow strip. In a wide plate or a stiffened wing box the skin, stringers and ribs hold the section flat, the sideways strain is prevented, and a transverse stress σ<sub>t</sub> = ν σ appears instead, with the same sign as σ: the tension skin is held wider than it wants to be. The skin then works biaxially, which matters for fatigue and buckling. σ = M y/I is unchanged; only the shape and the transverse stress differ. A wide plate held flat is also stiffer by 1/(1 − ν²) (see pure bending of thin plates).

examples.question: An aluminium alloy beam of symmetric I-section has E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, I = 8.5 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and depth 200 mm. A moment of 20 kN·m acts about its horizontal centroidal axis. Find (a) the largest direct stress, (b) the radius of curvature of the beam axis and (c) the free anticlastic radius of the cross-section.
steps: The section is symmetric, so the neutral axis is at mid-depth: y<sub>max</sub> = 200/2 = 100 mm = 0.100 m.
SI units: M = 2.0 × 10⁴ N·m, E = 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa.
(a) σ<sub>max</sub> = M y<sub>max</sub>/I = (2.0 × 10⁴ × 0.100)/(8.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.353 × 10⁸ Pa = 235.3 MPa, tension on one face and compression on the other.
Check with the section modulus: Z = I/y<sub>max</sub> = 8.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³, and M/Z = 2.0 × 10⁴/(8.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 235.3 MPa.
Strain check: ε = y<sub>max</sub>/R = 0.100/29.75 = 3.36 × 10⁻³, and σ/E = 235.3 × 10⁶/(7.0 × 10¹⁰) = 3.36 × 10⁻³. They agree.
(c) R′ = R/ν = 29.75/0.33 = 90.2 m, about three times R.
examples.answer: σ<sub>max</sub> = 235.3 MPa, R = 29.75 m and R′ = 90.2 m.

examples.question: A T-section spar cap has a flange 100 mm × 10 mm on top and a web 10 mm thick and 90 mm deep below it (total depth 100 mm). It carries a sagging moment of 3 kN·m (bottom fibres in tension), so M<sub>x</sub> = −3 kN·m in this book's convention. Find the neutral axis, I, the two section moduli and the top and bottom stresses. Which face yields first?
steps: Areas: flange A₁ = 1000 mm² with centroid 5 mm below the top; web A₂ = 900 mm² with centroid 10 + 45 = 55 mm below the top.
Centroid from the top: ȳ = (1000 × 5 + 900 × 55)/1900 = 28.68 mm. So y<sub>top</sub> = 28.68 mm and y<sub>bot</sub> = 100 − 28.68 = 71.32 mm.
Z<sub>top</sub> = I/y<sub>top</sub> = 62,754 mm³; Z<sub>bot</sub> = I/y<sub>bot</sub> = 25,240 mm³.
Top fibre, y = +28.68 mm: σ = M<sub>x</sub> y/I = (−3 × 10⁶ × 28.68)/1,800,044 = -47.8 N/mm² (compression).
examples.answer: The neutral axis is 28.68 mm below the top; I = 1,800,044 mm⁴; Z<sub>top</sub> = 62,754 mm³ and Z<sub>bot</sub> = 25,240 mm³. The top carries -47.8 MPa and the bottom +118.9 MPa, so the bottom fibre, 71.32 mm from the neutral axis, yields first.

traps: Measuring y from an outer face or the bottom of the web instead of from the centroidal neutral axis.
Using σ = M y/I when the moment is not about a principal axis; for a section with Ixy ≠ 0 use the methods of unsymmetrical bending.
Mixing units: M in kN·m with I in mm⁴. Work in N and mm (stress in N/mm² = MPa) or in N and m throughout.
Writing R′ = νR instead of R/ν. The anticlastic radius is larger than R, not smaller.
Giving the restrained transverse stress as −νσ. When the curl is prevented the transverse stress is +νσ, the same sign as σ.

quiz.q: State the assumptions of simple bending theory.
quiz.a: Plane sections stay plane and normal to the bent axis; small deflections; linear elastic material with the same E in tension and compression; the moment acts about a principal axis with no axial force.

quiz.q: Define the elastic section modulus and give its unit.
quiz.a: Z = I/y<sub>max</sub>, with I about the centroidal neutral axis and y<sub>max</sub> the distance to the farthest fibre. Unit m³ or mm³; σ<sub>max</sub> = M/Z.

quiz.q: Why does the neutral axis pass through the centroid in pure bending?
quiz.a: No axial force acts, so ∫σ dA = 0. With σ = E y/R this needs ∫y dA = 0, and the first moment of area is zero only about the centroid.

quiz.q: A beam has I = 12 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and y<sub>max</sub> = 150 mm. Find the largest stress for M = 30 kN·m.
An aluminium strip (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.30, thickness 2 mm) is bent to R = 20 m. Find the anticlastic radius and the transverse strain at the tension face.
quiz.a: R′ = R/ν = 20/0.30 = 66.7 m. At y = 1 mm the longitudinal strain is y/R = 0.001/20 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵, so the transverse strain is −ν y/R = −1.5 × 10⁻⁵: the tension face narrows.

quiz.q: A wing box and a plain strip of the same material bend to the same radius. Why does the strip curl and the box not, and what appears in the box instead?
quiz.a: The strip's edges are free, so the sideways strain −ν y/R curls it to R′ = R/ν. In the box the skin, stringers and ribs prevent that strain, so a transverse stress +νσ appears in the skin instead, which affects fatigue and buckling.

beyond: Anticlastic bending shows up as shape loss in thin panels and extra transverse stress at bonded repairs and cut-outs. In composite laminates a lay-up can couple bending in one direction with curvature in another. Search for "anticlastic curvature of plates" and "Searle parameter".

spec.aria: A T-section with a 100 by 10 millimetre flange and a 90 by 10 millimetre web, its neutral axis dashed 28.68 millimetres below the top and 71.32 millimetres above the bottom. Beside it a linear stress diagram: minus 47.8 megapascals compression at the top, plus 118.9 megapascals tension at the bottom, zero at the neutral axis. On the right, a rectangle and its curled shape after bending: the compression side widens, the tension side narrows, with anticlastic radius R prime equal to R over nu, 29.75 over 0.33 equals 90.2 metres in the first example.
